title: Brain Medicine in The News!
subtitle: It's already a big week for brain medicine, and it's only Wednesday.
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is a publication that advocates for a better future. In that future, we'll have brains that don't break down on their owners as often, and when they do, we fix them promptly. When you call a plumber, they don't judge you for having a sink. They don't look askance at your toilet. They look up the model and manufacturer and figure out what part you need to fix it. It's not a guessing game; you don't have to talk about it for a year. There's an established supply chain for plumbing, there's a licensed profession, and it works pretty smoothly.

Brain Medicine has not had the same smooth runway. We unfortunately split it up into psychiatry and separate neurology in the beginning. Then, along with our colleagues in anesthesia, we created the ability to perform neurosurgery, and neuroradiology became a separate specialty as well.

This is not just a range of specialties; it’s a diffusion of responsibility. Plumbers own the problem of getting water around your home. They work with distributors of goods that can fix a plumbing problem. Maybe you need a master plumber, but he’s still a plumber. There’s a regulation on what can be done in plumbing, just as there is with medicine. Brain medicine? It needs to be a lot more like plumbing—a straightforward discipline that combines the expertise necessary to move brain signals from one place to another, such that everything flows appropriately.

This is gonna take a change in public consciousness. We’re gonna stop talking about mental health—Mental health is just a subdomain of Brain Medicine.

The problem of mental health is not different than the problem of movement disorders, when it comes to the brain circuits and output of the brain. Depressed people wring their hands. They fidget. They have psychomotor retardation at other times. These are problems with movement. But we’re not calling it a movement disorder, we’re calling it a mental health problem. They can also be problems with gastric motility, indigestion, and constipation, which is a movement disorder of the gastrointestinal tract. OK, so sometimes it’s a movement disorder of smooth muscle control, and at other times it’s a movement disorder of skeletal muscle motor control. Sometimes we say things that don’t make any sense, despondent, disconnected, even psychotic, but at the end of the day, the brain represents feelings to our consciousness, and our motor control centers fire to create patterns of skeletal muscle activation that allow our tongue, jaw, larynx, and the like to make sounds.

Brain Medicine is our future terminal specialty that brings together the existing disciplines of psychology, psychiatry, neurology, neuroradiology, and neurosurgery, with all working together under one overarching umbrella. Why have an overarching umbrella? Because then you have an understanding of what the problem is, which tools can be brought to bear to solve it, and who to call. If your sink doesn’t work, you call a plumber. If your brain doesn’t work, you call a brain medicine doctor.

That’s the vision. This week, we’ve moved a little bit closer to getting the word out.

When I co-created RAMHT with Grady Hannah, it wasn’t obvious to us—yet—that “mental health” as a term was approaching the end of its lifespan, like the USB-A cable of its day. It is a live event, we’ve done it 5 times now, with 6 and 7 coming up! That having been said, it’s a hit event shaping this nascent field.

Get Tickets for RAMHT SF 2026 May 16th!

Check out press mentions of what we are up to at Radial, one such Brain Medicine company.

First, our own MaryEllen Eller spent time talking anxiety with the New York Post.

Then, Optum announced it would expand TMS coverage, allowing nurse practitioners in independent practice states to prescribe the first safe and effective treatment for brain disorders under this new brain medicine paradigm. Your own Owen Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, FCTMSS, was quoted in Behavioral Health Business News on the topic!

Then, along with Rob Glatter, M.D., your very own Editor Owen Muir, a 2022 Healio Healthcare Hero, co-authored two articles in Healio in the past two weeks! One on ketamine, and the other is about TMS in adolescents! Here is the highest data, but the rest of the articles are worth reading.

The most comprehensive meta-analysis on TMS to date, published in 2025 and encompassing 34 randomized controlled trials with 2,705 participants, demonstrated that TMS significantly reduced depression severity in children, adolescents and young adults with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of –1.55 (95% CI, –1.88 to –1.23).

Another recent Healio article noted that neuromodulation is coming to the home!

FDA Approval: Approved under PMA P250010, the Proliv™Rx system is indicated for adults with MDD who have not adequately improved from traditional antidepressant medication.

“To say we have an unmet need for effective, evidence-based home-use treatments in psychiatry is an understatement,” Linda L. Carpenter, MD, lead study author and professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University, told Healio.

Next, I have to get to a meeting with our friends at Compass Pathways to talk about how we're going to get psychedelic medicines like COMP360 to the world.

They are, just yesterday, announcing a grant program for training in psychedelic medicine:

Through the grant program, Compass expects to award up to three organizations grants to support the development of foundational psychedelic and COMP360-specific training. Applications will be accepted from April 14 through May 14, 2026. Interested organizations can apply here: training-grants.compasspathways.com.

“As we prepare for the potential commercial launch of COMP360 for treatment-resistant depression, our priority is ensuring that healthcare providers are trained, confident, and ready to deliver COMP360 treatment responsibly where eligible patients may receive care,” said Dr. Steve Levine, Chief Patient Officer at Compass Pathways. “Through this grant program, we look forward to collaborating with credible and experienced training organizations to develop high-quality content to ensure multidisciplinary teams of providers are ready to deliver psilocybin treatment at scale, if approved.

Thus, I'd better wrap this up!

We may be the first, but we already have friends working with us in the space!

Salma Health, BrainsWay, Definium Therapeutics, Mindful Health Solutions, Beacon Biosignals, Radial, Graymatters Health, NRx Pharmaceuticals, Inc., MDHub, Beckley Clinical, Hydra Strategies, Harvard/MGH Program in Refugee Trauma, Cover My Mental Health, and that is just friends at the next RAMHT event.

Brain medicine is a movement; let's all get on board.
